issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, 'Similar cars' is hard to justify as a salient trigger unless the disaster specifically involved a vehicle context, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other triggers ('feeling physically unwell', 'unpredictable situations') and the negative appraisals describe generalized vulnerability and loss of control, but 'similar cars' introduces a highly specific cue that does not cohere with the rest of the formulation or trauma type.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'Alcohol smell' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless supported by memory or threat content linking alcohol odor to the disaster context. Here there are no Memory or Threat items providing that connection, making this trigger clinically incoherent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: The formulation shows a strong Triggers → Negative Appraisals link, but the selected trigger items mostly imply internal-state or unpredictability cues, whereas 'I have to be on guard all the time' implies an ongoing external danger/threat style response. With Threat node absent and no trigger content clearly tied to vigilance for danger, this appraisal is weakly matched to the trigger pattern and stands out as formulation-incongruent in this profile.

vignette:
When Dara Lim was 51, a fast-moving wildfire tore through the foothill community where he and his wife had been staying with relatives for a long holiday weekend. He had stepped outside at dusk because the air felt strangely heavy and the sky had turned an unnatural orange. Within minutes the smell of smoke thickened, ash began falling across the driveway, and the wind kept shifting in ways no one could predict. He remembered trying to decide whether to pack the car or wait for more information, moving from room to room and feeling his own judgment slipping as different neighbors shouted different plans. By the time they left, visibility was poor and the roads were clogged with other families. What stayed with him most was not only the fire itself but the sense that the world had become dangerously unstable in an instant, and that when things turned chaotic he could not trust himself to know what to do.

In the weeks after they returned home, Dara found that certain moments pulled him back into that night with surprising force. If he woke with a headache, a brief feverish feeling, or the heaviness of a cold coming on, he became frightened by how quickly his body could feel out of control; being physically unwell stirred the same helplessness he had felt as the smoke closed in. The smell of smoke was especially potent. Even ordinary situations—a neighbor using a grill, a faint burnt odor from an office microwave, the sharp scent from a city bus passing his building—could make his chest tighten and his thoughts race. Unpredictable situations unsettled him in the same way. A sudden change in plans, a delayed train, an unexpected agenda shift at work all carried a charge far beyond the moment itself, as if uncertainty were proof that danger could escalate before he had time to think.

These experiences quickly fed the conclusions he had begun drawing about himself. Dara had come to believe that he could not rely on himself when things were not fully under control. He replayed the evacuation and focused on every hesitation, convinced those seconds meant something deeply wrong about him. When his reactions surged around smoke or sudden disruptions, he became afraid that he was going crazy. What frightened him most was how disproportionate it seemed even to him: he could be standing in his office in Washington, reviewing policy briefs, and still feel as if one odd smell or one unforeseen complication could tip him into panic. From there he became certain he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. He watched for signs that something might go wrong, scanning the air, the weather, traffic reports, and even his own body for the earliest hint of trouble.

That way of living made the triggers spread through more of his days. At work as a policy analyst, he had always tolerated ambiguity as part of the job, but now last-minute changes from supervisors or shifting deadlines felt intolerable. The more he told himself that only constant vigilance could keep him safe, the more any unpredictable situation stood out immediately and felt dangerous. He noticed the smell of overheated electronics in a conference room before anyone else did and could not concentrate for the rest of the meeting. If he felt run-down during the day, he tracked every bodily sensation, and the mere fact of noticing it seemed to confirm that he was no longer mentally steady. In those moments he would think that a capable person would stay calm, whereas he was falling apart. His beliefs about being unreliable and possibly losing his mind made each trigger feel more significant, not less.

At home, his wife had begun to see how narrow his world was becoming. Dara insisted on checking air-quality apps repeatedly and wanted clear exit plans before visiting friends or attending family gatherings. He disliked spontaneous outings and grew tense if anyone suggested changing plans at the last minute. He understood that others saw these precautions as excessive, but to him they felt necessary; if disaster could arrive without warning once, he believed only relentless care stood between his family and another catastrophe. Yet each effort to stay prepared seemed to make him more sensitive to smoke, bodily discomfort, and uncertainty, until ordinary life felt laced with threat.

He sought help after leaving an important meeting when someone burned popcorn in the office kitchen. The smell hit him, and with it came the conviction that his reaction meant he was losing his mind in a way he could no longer hide. He was ashamed that he no longer trusted himself in exactly the settings where he had once felt most competent. Sitting in the intake, Dara said he wanted to feel dependable again, but he was afraid that the damage had already been done and that the next unpredictable moment would prove he could not hold himself together.
